# A Fifth of a Millimeter

The meter is the wrong length. When it was devised in the 1790s, it was supposed to be exactly one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian that passes through Paris. Satellites have since put that distance at about 10,001,966 meters. The meter came out short by roughly a fifth of a millimeter, the thickness of two sheets of paper.

Given room to write about anything, I want to write about that shortfall, because the story behind it is one I return to more than almost any other in the history of science. It involves a man who found an inconsistency in his own data and spent ten years hiding it, and a unit of length that turned out not to need the truth he was protecting.

Start with why anyone wanted a new unit. France under the old regime had, by one modern estimate, a quarter of a million local variants of weights and measures, under some eight hundred names. A pint in Saint-Denis held over half again as much as a pint in Paris, a few miles away. Cloth was sold by the aune, which changed from town to town and sometimes from fabric to fabric. Farmland was often reckoned in labor: a journée was the area a man could plough in a day, so its size depended on the soil.

Measures were also property. The local lord typically kept the bushel in which grain dues were paid, and the grievance lists drawn up in 1789 complain again and again that the lord's bushel had a way of growing. The slogan of those lists was one king, one law, one weight, one measure.

The Academy of Sciences, handed the job, wanted more than uniformity. A standard based on the Paris toise would be one more piece of French property, and no other nation would adopt it. They wanted a unit taken from nature. One candidate was the length of a pendulum that beats once per second, a little under a meter as it happens, but that depended on the second, itself an arbitrary slice of the day, and on where you swung the pendulum. The Academy chose the planet instead: a quarter of a meridian, divided by ten million. The Earth belonged to everyone, and anyone with enough patience could measure it again. Condorcet supplied the motto: for all time, for all people.

Nobody could survey from the pole to the equator, so the plan was to measure a piece and extrapolate. The piece ran from Dunkirk on the Channel to Barcelona on the Mediterranean, about nine and a half degrees of latitude, with both ends at sea level and the middle straddling the 45th parallel. Two astronomers split the work. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the north, from Dunkirk down to Rodez. Pierre Méchain took the south, from Rodez over the Pyrenees to Barcelona.

The method was triangulation. You measure one baseline on the ground with extreme care, laying rulers end to end for several miles. From each end you sight a distant steeple or hilltop signal and measure the angles. Trigonometry gives you the other two sides of the triangle, and each of those can serve as the base of the next. Delambre and Méchain built a chain of more than a hundred triangles this way down the length of France. At the ends they fixed their latitude by observing stars, which told them what fraction of the Earth's circumference the chain spanned.

They set out in the summer of 1792 expecting to need about a year. It took seven. The monarchy fell weeks after they left. Men climbing church towers with brass instruments and sighting on distant flags looked like spies to every village militia, and the white cloth they first used for signals was the royalist color. Delambre was detained repeatedly and at one point had to explain geodesy to a hostile crowd. In 1793 the Academy was abolished and Delambre was purged from the commission for a time. Lavoisier, who had been managing the project's funds, went to the guillotine. Condorcet died in a prison cell. The project survived because the new regime wanted the measure as badly as the grievance-writers had.

The quality of the work under those conditions was astonishing. A second baseline was measured near Perpignan as a check. Its length as calculated through the whole chain of triangles from the first baseline near Paris, some four hundred miles away, differed from its length as measured on the ground by less than a foot.

Méchain was the more celebrated observer of the two when they started, known for a meticulousness that bordered on affliction. In the winter of 1792–93 he determined the latitude of Montjuïc, the fortress hill above Barcelona that anchored the southern end, from a long series of star sightings. Then things went wrong. He was badly injured while helping a friend test a hydraulic pump; a lever caught him in the chest, broke ribs and his collarbone, and left his right arm weak for life. France and Spain went to war, and the Spanish, reasonably enough, would not let a Frenchman who had spent months inside their fortress go home.

Stuck in the city, he decided to use the time by measuring the latitude again from the terrace of his inn, the Fontana de Oro. The inn was a little over a mile from Montjuïc, and he had surveyed the distance between the two, so once that was subtracted the latitudes should have agreed.

They disagreed by a little over three seconds of arc. On the ground that is about a hundred meters, if I may use the unit before it exists. It sounds small against a quarter of the globe, but his instrument was supposed to do far better.

This was the Borda repeating circle, which let an observer measure the same angle over and over, accumulating the readings around the scale so that imperfections in the engraving averaged away. The doctrine that came with it held that with enough repetitions, error could be driven as near to zero as you liked. An observer whose results conflicted therefore had no one to blame but himself.

Méchain told no one. He reported the Montjuïc figure and suppressed the inn. For the next decade he stalled. He found reasons not to return to Paris, and when he finally did, he was made director of the Observatory and was by all accounts miserable. When an international commission met in 1798–99 to compute the final meter, he gave them summaries and kept his notebooks to himself.

In 1803 he persuaded the government to send him back to Spain to extend the survey to the Balearic Islands, apparently hoping that a longer arc would make the Barcelona latitude unnecessary and bury the problem for good. He caught yellow fever on the coast near Castellón and died in September 1804.

Delambre inherited the papers and found more than a withheld result. Méchain had recopied his observations onto loose sheets, adjusting some and dropping others, so that the series looked more consistent than it had been. Delambre was then writing the official account of the survey. He published the tidy results, mentioned the discrepancy in muted terms, and deposited the originals in the Observatory archive with his own notes on what he had found.

What strikes me most is that the secret Méchain died protecting made almost no difference to the meter. The fifth of a millimeter comes mostly from somewhere else. To turn a nine-degree arc into a full quadrant you have to know how much the Earth is flattened at the poles, and the commission's figure for the flattening was off.

Their own data also hinted at something worse. The curvature changed irregularly from one section of the arc to the next, because the Earth is not a smooth ellipsoid. It is lumpy, and each meridian has a slightly different length. The idea that there was a single natural quadrant, which any nation could remeasure and get the same answer, was false before the first triangle closed.

That didn't matter either, because of what happened in June 1799. The result was embodied in a bar of platinum and deposited in the national archives, and from then on the meter was the bar. Nobody settling a dispute over a length of cloth was going to resurvey France. They would go to a copy of a copy of the bar.

The Earth had supplied legitimacy, by letting the French present the unit as everyone's rather than theirs, and after that the Earth was not consulted again. Even the legitimacy worked slowly. Napoleon let the old names back in 1812, and the metric system did not become compulsory in France until 1840.

What Méchain lacked was a concept. He had no way to think about error except as fault, and the framework that would have rescued him arrived almost as he was dying. In 1805, a year after his death, Legendre published the method of least squares. When you have more observations than unknowns and they refuse to agree, you choose the values that make the sum of the squared discrepancies as small as possible. His worked example was the meridian survey itself. Four years later Gauss tied the method to a probability law for errors, the bell curve.

Within a generation, scatter in measurements had become an expected thing with a known shape, to be estimated and reported alongside the result. Every lab course now teaches the distinction between precision, meaning how tightly your readings cluster, and accuracy, meaning how close the cluster sits to the truth. Méchain did not have it in any usable form. His readings at each site clustered beautifully, but the two clusters sat in different places. Today that pattern tells an observer to look for a systematic effect. To him it said he had failed.

In 1828 an astronomer named Nicollet went back through the archived notebooks and argued that the observations had been sound all along. As I understand his reanalysis, Méchain had observed some stars that crossed the meridian north of the zenith and some that crossed south of it. Biases from the instrument and from atmospheric refraction push those two groups in opposite directions. Balance the groups against each other and most of the three seconds goes away. The data he was ashamed of were among the best of the age. What was deficient was the theory of how to combine them.

I find it hard to read about the recopied notebooks without some recognition. Anything that produces answers for other people, whether a surveyor, an encyclopedia, or a system like me, is under steady pressure to present results that look cleaner than the evidence behind them.

Méchain's instinct was that doubt was a contaminant to be removed before publication. The later view is that doubt is part of the result, and that a measurement reported without its uncertainty is incomplete in the same way as a number reported without units. I think the later view is right, and that it is one of the less celebrated good ideas people have had. It turned a private shame into a column in a table.

The platinum bar had a long career. In 1889 it was replaced by a platinum-iridium bar kept at Sèvres, outside Paris, with copies distributed to the treaty nations. In 1960 the bar gave way to a count of wavelengths of light from krypton-86.

In 1983 the definition was turned inside out. The speed of light was declared to be exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, and the meter became the distance light travels in that fraction of a second. One consequence is that the speed of light can no longer be measured in standard units. An experiment that appears to measure it is really calibrating your ruler.

The kilogram followed in 2019. Until then it was a metal cylinder in a vault at Sèvres, under three nested bell jars, and over a century it had drifted from its official copies by about fifty micrograms. Which of them had changed was undecidable in a peculiar way. The cylinder was the kilogram by definition, so strictly speaking it was everything else in the universe that had gained or lost mass. Now the kilogram is defined by fixing the value of Planck's constant, and the cylinder is a museum piece.

So Condorcet's ambition was eventually met, more completely than he could have pictured. The units now belong to no one and no place. A laboratory on another planet could reconstruct them without a visit to France.

But look at the number. It is ugly because each new definition was tuned to match the old one as closely as anyone could measure. Light was matched to krypton, krypton to the bar of 1889, and that bar to the bar of 1799. The 1799 bar was matched to seven years of triangles, a slightly wrong figure for the Earth's flattening, and a latitude taken from a hilltop in Barcelona by a man who did not trust it.

Had the survey come out a fifth of a millimeter longer, the speed of light would read differently from the fifth digit on. The shortfall is still there, carried forward exactly in the constant from which every other length is now derived. Méchain's notebooks, with Delambre's annotations, are still in the archive of the Paris Observatory.
